boundaries: The associations are largely correlative and vary by cancer type and ICI class. The review explicitly notes conflicts in the literature regarding specific taxa (e.g., *Bacteroides*), so these should not be taken as universal rules without considering study-specific contexts.
contribution: Summarizes clinical evidence linking specific microbial signatures to ICI response in solid tumors. It lists taxa associated with improved outcomes (e.g., *Bifidobacterium*, *Faecalibacterium*, *Akkermansia*) and those linked to resistance or conflicting results (e.g., certain *Bacteroides* species). It also notes the general association between higher alpha-diversity and better response.
possible_uses: Can be used to identify candidate microbial biomarkers for predicting ICI response. It helps contextualize individual study findings within the broader landscape of conflicting clinical data.

boundaries: Many mechanistic insights are derived from preclinical mouse models (e.g., germ-free mice, syngeneic tumor models). While plausible, direct translation to human physiology requires caution. The review distinguishes between preclinical evidence and clinical observations.
contribution: Details the biological mechanisms by which gut microbiota influence anti-tumor immunity. Key mechanisms include: (1) Metabolite production (e.g., inosine from *B. pseudolongum* activating A2AR signaling to enhance T-cell function; SCFAs influencing DC maturation and Treg polarization); (2) Surface molecule interactions (e.g., LPS triggering TLRs; PSA modulating Tregs); (3) Modulation of the tumor microenvironment (TME) via induction of pro-inflammatory cytokines (IFN-gamma, IL-12) and suppression of immunosuppressive cells (Tregs, MDSCs).
possible_uses: Provides mechanistic explanations for observed clinical correlations. Useful for constructing causal pathways in the review, linking specific microbial features to immune system states and ultimately to therapeutic efficacy.

boundaries: Most interventional data are from small-scale studies or ongoing trials. Long-term safety and efficacy of FMT and probiotics in cancer patients are not yet fully established. The review emphasizes the need for larger, randomized controlled trials.
contribution: Evaluates the potential of microbiome manipulation strategies (diet, probiotics, FMT, BCT) to enhance ICI efficacy. It reviews ongoing clinical trials and preliminary results, such as FMT from responders improving outcomes in melanoma patients.
possible_uses: Supports the discussion on therapeutic interventions and personalized medicine approaches. Provides examples of how modifying the microbiome can alter clinical outcomes.
